newsitem.title: USA: U.S. medicare fund may go bankrupt by 2001.
newsitem.headline: U.S. medicare fund may go bankrupt by 2001.

text.p: Medicare's trustees predicted on Thursday the program's hospital trust fund would be bankrupt in 2001 without major reforms -- the same dire outlook issued last year.

In releasing the annual trustees' report, Health Secretary Donna Shalala said the financial prognosis for the program was marginally better in 1996, due to a slowdown in home health care and other fast-growing parts of Medicare.
But she warned that Democrats and Republicans were running out of time to craft a bipartisan solution to fix the popular insurance program for 38 million senior citizens.
"The bad news is that 2001 is one year closer today than it was when we issued our last report," Shalala said.
"We cannot afford to delay and delay ... it is time for us to provide the American people, especially senior citizens and those with disabilities, the peace of mind they deserve," she said.
The White House and congressional Republicans have been sparring over possible Medicare cuts as they try to work out a balanced budget deal.

President Clinton has recommended $100 billion in Medicare cuts over five years. Nearly all the reductions would come from doctors, hospitals, managed care plans and other health providers while carefully sparing beneficiaries any pain.
A new analysis released Thursday by Medicare actuaries said Clinton's plan would keep the program solvent until 2008.

During the last session of Congress Republicans called for $270 billion in Medicare cuts over seven years, as part of a failed balanced budget plan. They were attacked in the 1996 elections by Democrats who charged their proposal would have hurt beneficiaries and gutted the program.
This time around Republicans are being more cautious. They have yet to put forth a reform plan of their own and want the White House to go first on any beneficiary cuts.

Republicans used Thursday's report to bolster their case for major Medicare reforms, holding a Senate news conference to criticize Democrats and call for change even before the trustees' findings were formally announced.
"If we don't move forward in a resolute, bipartisan manner, we will never put Medicare back on the road to recovery," Tennessee Republican Sen. Bill Frist said.
House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, said he was optimistic a Medicare agreement could be reached shortly if the president resists pressure from liberal Democrats.

The troubled Medicare Part A trust fund covers hospital, home health and over services. It is funded through 2.9 percent payroll tax, equally divided between employers and employees and is projected to run a $23.4 billion deficit in 2001.
The trustees also warned spending was growing too quickly in Medicare Part B, which funds doctors' visits and other outpatient care, but is in no danger of bankruptcy.
